title: The rich young man (Mark 10:17–22)
hook: Jesus looked at him and loved him, then asked for everything

segments.voice: Yesterday, the disciples shooed the children away, and he took them in his arms. Your line was like a child. Did you receive something without deflecting it? Day two hundred two.

Jesus is setting out on the road again when a man comes running up. Grown men didn't run much in that world; it wasn't dignified. This one runs, and kneels in the dust, and asks the biggest question there is. "Good Master, what shall I do that I may inherit eternal life?" Jesus pushes back on the compliment first: why call me good? No one is good but God alone. Then he lists the commandments everybody knows. Don't kill, don't commit adultery, don't steal, don't bear false witness, don't defraud, honor your father and mother. And the man says, sincerely, I've kept all these since I was young. He isn't boasting. He's a good man. And he still feels something's missing, or he wouldn't have run.
screen: `A MAN COMES RUNNING.` → `WHAT SHALL I DO?` → `I'VE KEPT THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "Then Jesus beholding him loved him, and said unto him, One thing thou lackest: go thy way, sell whatsoever thou hast, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, take up the cross, and follow me." Look at the order. First he looks at him. Then he loves him. Only then does he ask the hardest thing. Mark is the only gospel that says Jesus loved him. Matthew and Luke tell the story and leave it out. And by the way, Mark never says he was young. Matthew calls him a young man, and Luke calls him a ruler. Our title stitches the Gospels together. Then the saddest line: "And he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions." He doesn't argue. He doesn't sneer. He just can't do it, and walks away sad. And Jesus lets him go. What happened to him after? The Gospels are silent. Christians read the command in more than one way. Some have taken it literally: the early monk Anthony of Egypt, the story goes, heard this read in church and gave away his family's land. Many others read it as aimed at this one man, and at whatever holds any of us back from following. Almost everyone notices the love. The hard word wasn't a rejection. It came from someone who had looked at him closely and loved what he saw.
screen: `HE LOOKED, AND LOVED, AND ASKED.` · `ONLY MARK SAYS HE LOVED HIM.` · `HE WENT AWAY GRIEVED.` · `LITERAL, OR AIMED AT HIS HEART?` · then, large: `JESUS BEHOLDING HIM LOVED HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look before you advise. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you'd like to tell something to. Advice, a correction, a hard truth. Before any of that, just look at them in your mind. Their face. What they're carrying. What they're good at. Stay there until you feel something like love for them, even a little. If you pray, you can ask to see them the way Jesus looked at the man. Only then, if you still need to, decide what you'd say. The bell holds the time.
The rich young man. A good man who ran to Jesus, was loved, was asked for everything, and walked away sad.
Your line: he loved him. Today, before you give anyone advice, look at them first, long enough to love them. Day two hundred two.

screen: `DAY 202 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A CAMEL AND A NEEDLE.`

howItsDone: Some Christians, especially in monastic orders, take vows of poverty inspired by this story; many others read it as a call to examine what holds them back, and to give generously to the poor.

fork.setup: you're the man. you've kept every commandment since youth. Jesus looks at you with love and says: sell everything, give it to the poor, and follow me. what do you do?
fork.reveal: "he was sad at that saying, and went away grieved: for he had great possessions." and Jesus let him go, still loved.

original.note: Greek: he loved, from agapaō. Mark 10:21: Jesus looked at him and loved him.

trapdoor: what you thought: rich people can't follow Jesus.
what it means: Jesus looks, loves, and only then asks for everything; the man walks away sad, and is let go.
what a scholar hears: only Mark says he loved him, and only Matthew calls him young: the famous title is a blend of three Gospels.

notes: 'Grown men didn't run much in that world; it wasn't dignified' is a common commentary observation; confirm or soften.
'Don't defraud' in the commandment list is unique to Mark (10:19). Not highlighted in the script.
Antony of Egypt: Athanasius says he heard the Gospel (the Matthew 19:21 form) read in church and gave away his inherited land. Script says 'the story goes'. Confirm.
Index title 'The rich young man' is kept, and the script explains it blends Matthew (young) and Luke (ruler).
